la:noun:animus.gloss: life, life force, soul, vitality (that life-giving aspect which animates a thing)
senses: life, life force, soul, vitality (that life-giving aspect which animates a thing)
conscience, intellect, mind, reason, sensibility, understanding (the intellectual dimension of the human mind in general; the seat of the rational and other thoughts a person experiences)
heart, mind, spirit (the affective dimension of the human mind in general; the seat of the emotions and feelings a person experiences)
affect, emotion, feeling, impulse, passion (the essence of that which is situated within the affective mind)

certain particular emotional aspects of one's affective makeup: affection; aggression; courage; pride; will (“firmity or fixity of purpose”), determination, firmness, resoluteness, resolve; wrath, anger, ire
motive, motivation, reason (any intellectually or emotionally based incentive to act in a particular manner)
aim, aspiration, design, idea, intent, intention, plan, purpose, resolution (that which exists in the mind as a formulation, and causes a subject to act or to behave in a particular manner)
disposition, inclination, nature, temperament (the inherent emotional disposition of a human being, by extension of the affective dimension)
affect, mood, temper (the instant mental state of a human being)
beloved. dearest, heart, soul (as a term of endearment)
la:noun:animus.html:
ănĭmus, i, m.
a Graeco-Italic form of ἄνεμος = wind (as ego, lego, of ἐγώ, λέγω); cf. Sanscr. an = to breathe, anas = breath, anilas = wind; Goth. uz-ana = exspiro; Erse, anal = breath; Germ. Unst = a storm (so, sometimes); but Curt. does not extend the connection to ΑΩ, ἄημι = to blow; a modification of animus—by making which the Romans took a step in advance of the Greeks, who used ἡ ψυχή for both these ideas—is anima, which has the physical meaning of ἄνεμος, so that Cic. was theoretically right, but historically wrong, when he said, ipse animus ab animā dictus est, Tusc. 1, 9, 19; after the same analogy we have from ψύχω = to breathe, blow, ψυχή = breath, life, soul; from πνέω = to breathe, πνεῦμα = air, breath, life, in class. Greek, and = spirit, a spiritual being, in Hellenistic Greek; from spiro = to breathe, blow, spiritus = breath, breeze, energy, high spirit, and poet. and post-Aug. = soul, mind; the Engl. ghost = Germ. Geist may be comp. with Germ. giessen and χέω, to pour, and for this interchange of the ideas of gases and liquids, cf. : insula adspiratur freto Gallico, is flowed upon, washed, by the Gallic Strait; the Sanscr. ātman = breath, soul, with which comp. ἀϋτμή = breath; Germ. Odem = breath, and Athem = breath, soul, with which group Curt. connects αὔω, ἄημι; the Heb. = breath, life, soul; and = breath, wind, life, spirit, soul or mind
.
In a general sense, the rational soul in man (in opp. to the body, corpus, and to the physical life, anima), ἡ ψυχή: humanus animus decerptus ex mente divinā,: Corpus animum praegravat, Atque affixit humo divinae particulam aurae,: credo deos immortales sparsisse animos in corpora humana, ut essent qui terras tuerentur etc.,: eas res tueor animi non corporis viribus,; so : quae (res) vel infirmis corporibus animo tamen administratur,; : omnes animi cruciatus et corporis,: levantes Corpus et animum,: formam et figuram animi magis quam corporis complecti,; : animi validus et corpore ingens,: Aristides primus animum pinxit et sensus hominis expressit, quae vocantur Graece ethe, item perturbationes,first painted the soul, put a soul into his figures, (cf.: animosa signa,life-like statues,): si nihil esset in eo (animo), nisi id, ut per eum viveremus, i. e. were it mere anima, : Singularis est quaedam natura atque vis animi, sejuncta ab his usitatis notisque naturis, i. e. the four material elements,: Neque nos corpora sumus. Cum igitur nosce te dicit, hoc dicit, nosce animum tuum, : In quo igitur loco est (animus)? Credo equidem in capite,: corpora nostra, terreno principiorum genere confecta, ardore animi concalescunt,derive their heat from the fiery nature of the soul,: Non valet tantum animus, ut se ipsum ipse videat: at, ut oculus, sic animus, se non videns alia cernit,: foramina illa (the senses), quae patent ad animum a corpore, callidissimo artificio natura fabricata est, : dum peregre est animus sine corpore velox, independently of the body, i. e. the mind roaming in thought, : discessus animi a corpore,; : cum nihil erit praeter animum,when there shall be nothing but the soul, when the soul shall be disembodied,; so, animus vacans corpore,; and: animus sine corpore,: sine mente animoque nequit residere per artus pars ulla animaï, (for the pleonasm here, v.infra, II. A. 1.): Reliquorum sententiae spem adferunt posse animos, cum e corporibus excesserint in caelum pervenire,: permanere animos arbitramur consensu nationum omnium,: Pherecydes primus dixit animos esse hominum sempiternos,: Quod ni ita se haberet, ut animi immortales essent, haud etc.,: immortalitas animorum, ; ; : aeternitas animorum,; 1, 22, 50 (for the plur. animorum, in this phrase, cf. ); for the atheistic notions about the soul, v. Lucr. bk. iii.—
In a more restricted sense, the mind as thinking, feeling, willing, the intellect, the sensibility, and the will, acc. to the almost universally received division of the mental powers since the time of Kant (Diog. Laert. 8, 30, says that Pythagoras divided ἡ ψυχή into ὁ νοῦς, αἱ φρένες, and ὁ θυμός; and that man had ὁ νοῦς and ὁ θυμός in common with other animals, but he alone had αἱ φρένες. Here ὁ νοῦς and ὁ θυμός must denote the understanding and the sensibility, and αἱ φρένες, the reason. Plutarch de Placit. 4, 21, says that the Stoics called the supreme faculty of the mind (τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν τῆς ψυχῆς) ὁ λογισμός, reason. Cic. sometimes speaks of a twofold division; as, Est animus in partes tributus duas, quarum altera rationis est particeps, altera expers (i. e. τὸ λογιστικόν and τὸ ἄλογον of Plato; cf. ), i. e. the reason or intellect and the sensibility, Tusc. 2, 21, 47; so ; ; ; and again of a threefold; as, Plato triplicem finxit animum, cujus principatum, id est rationem in capite sicut in arce posuit, et duas partes (the two other parts) ei parere voluit, iram et cupiditatem, quas locis disclusit; iram in pectore, cupiditatem subter praecordia locavit, i. e. the reason or intellect, and the sensibility here resolved into desire and aversion, ; so . The will, ἡ βούλησις, voluntas, arbitrium, seems to have been sometimes merged in the sensibility, ὁ θυμός, animus, animi, sensus, and sometimes identified with the intellect or reason, ὁ νοῦς, ὁ λογισμός, mens, ratio).
The general power of perception and thought, the reason, intellect, mind (syn.: mens, ratio, ingenium), ὁ νοῦς: cogito cum meo animo,; so : cum animis vestris cogitare,: recordari cum animo,; and without cum: animo meditari,; cf. : cogitare volvereque animo,: animo cogitare,: statuere apud animum,: proposui in animo meo,: nisi me animus fallit, hi sunt, etc.,: in dubio est animus,; prol. 1; cf. : animum ad se ipsum advocamus,: lumen animi, ingenii consiliique tui,— For the sake of rhet. fulness, animus often has a synonym joined with it: Mens et animus et consilium et sententia civitatis posita est in legibus,: magnam cui mentem animumque Delius inspirat vates,: complecti animo et cogitatione,; : animis et cogitatione comprehendere,: cum omnia ratione animoque lustraris,: animorum ingeniorumque naturale quoddam quasi pabulum consideratio naturae,.—Hence the expressions: agitatio animi, attentio, contentio; animi adversio; applicatio animi; judicium, opinio animorum, etc. (v. these vv.); and animum advertere, adjungere, adplicare, adpellere, inducere, etc. (v. these vv.).—
Of particular faculties of mind, the memory: etiam nunc mihi Scripta illa dicta sunt in animo Chrysidis,: An imprimi, quasi ceram, animum putamus etc. (an idea of Aristotle's),: ex animo effluere,: omnia fert aetas, animum quoque; ... Nunc oblita mihi tot carmina,.—
Consciousness (physically considered) or the vital power, on which consciousness depends ( = conscientia, q. v. II. A., or anima, q. v. II. E.): vae miserae mihi. Animo malest: aquam velim,I'm fainting, my wits are going,; : reliquit animus Sextium gravibus acceptis vulneribus,: Unā eademque viā sanguis animusque sequuntur,: animusque reliquit euntem,: nisi si timor abstulit omnem Sensum animumque,: linqui deinde animo et submitti genu coepit,: repente animo linqui solebat, Suet. : ad recreandos defectos animo puleio,.—
The conscience, in mal. part. (v. conscientia, II. B. 2. b.): cum conscius ipse animus se remordet,: quos conscius animus exagitabat,: suae malae cogitationes conscientiaeque animi terrent,.—
In Plaut. very freq., and once also in Cic., meton. for judicium, sententia, opinion, judgment; mostly meo quidem animo or meo animo, according to my mind, in my opinion, : e meo quidem animo aliquanto facias rectius, si, etc.,: meo quidem animo, hic tibi hodie evenit bonus,; so ; ; ; ; ; ; : edepol lenones meo animo novisti,: nisi, ut meus est animus, fieri non posse arbitror, (cf.: EX MEI ANIMI SENTENTIA,: ex animi tui sententiā,).—
The imagination, the fancy (for which Cic. often uses cogitatio, as Ac. 2, 15, 48): cerno animo sepultam patriam, miseros atque insepultos acervos civium,: fingere animo jubebat aliquem etc.,: Fingite animis; litterae enim sunt cogitationes nostrae, et quae volunt, sic intuentur, ut ea cernimus, quae videmus,: Nihil animo videre poterant,.—
The power of feeling, the sensibility, the heart, the feelings, affections, inclinations, disposition, passions (either honorable or base; syn.: sensus, adfectus, pectus, cor), ὁ θυμός.
In gen., heart, soul, spirit, feeling, inclination, affection, passion: Medea, animo aegra, amore saevo saucia, Enn. ap. Auct. ad (cf. : animo hercle homo suo est miser): tu si animum vicisti potius quam animus te, est quod gaudeas, etc.,-29: harum scelera et lacrumae confictae dolis Redducunt animum aegrotum ad misericordiam,: Quo gemitu conversi animi (sunt),: Hoc fletu concussi animi,; 4, 310: animum offendere,; ; so .—Mens and animus are often conjoined and contrasted, mind and heart (cf. the Homeric κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν, in mind and heart): mentem atque animum delectat suum, entertains his mind and delights his heart, Enn. ap. : Satin tu sanus mentis aut animi tui?: mala mens, malus animus,bad mind, bad heart,: animum et mentem meam ipsā cogitatione hominum excellentium conformabam,: Nec vero corpori soli subveniendum est, sed menti atque animo multo magis,: ut omnium mentes animosque perturbaret,; : Istuc mens animusque fert,: Stare Socrates dicitur tamquam quodam recessu mentis atque animi facto a corpore,; .— And very rarely with this order inverted: Jam vero animum ipsum mentemque hominis, etc.,: mente animoque nobiscum agunt,: quem nobis animum, quas mentes imprecentur,; and sometimes pleon. without such distinction: in primis regina quietum Accipit in Teucros animum mentemque benignam,a quiet mind and kindly heart,; so, pravitas animi atque ingenii, (for mens et animus, etc., in the sense of thought, used as a pleonasm, v.supra, II. A. 1.): Verum animus ubi semel se cupiditate devinxit malā, etc.,: animus perturbatus et incitatus nec cohibere se potest, nec quo loco vult insistere,: animum comprimit,: animus alius ad alia vitia propensior,; : sed quid ego hic animo lamentor,: tremere animo,: ingentes animo concipit iras,: exsultare animo,.—So often ex animo, from the heart, from the bottom of one's heart, deeply, truly, sincerely: Paulum interesse censes ex animo omnia facias an de industriā?from your heart or with some design,; : nisi quod tibi bene ex animo volo,: verbum

ex animo dicere, : sive ex animo id fit sive simulate,: majore studio magisve ex animo petere non possum,: ex animo vereque diligi,: ex animo dolere,: quae (gentes) dederunt terram meam sibi cum gaudio et toto corde et ex animo,; ; Pet. 5, 3.—And with gen.

With verbs: Quid illam miseram animi excrucias?; : Antipho me excruciat animi,: discrucior animi,: in spe pendebit animi,: juvenemque animi miserata repressit, pitying him in her heart, θυμῷ φιλέουσά τε κηδομένη τε (Hom. Il. 1, 196), .—
With adjj.: aeger animi,; ; ; ; : infelix animi,: felix animi,: victus animi,: ferox animi,: promptus animi,: praestans animi,: ingens animi, (for this gen. v. Ramsh. Gr. p. 323; Key, § 935; Wagner ad ; Draeger, Hist. Synt. I. p. 443).—
Meton., disposition, character (so, often ingenium): nimis paene animo es Molli, Pac. ap. : animo audaci proripit sese, Rib.: petulans protervo, iracundo animo,; : ubi te vidi animo esse omisso (omisso = neglegenti, Don.),; fin.: promptus animus vester,: animis estis simplicibus et mansuetis nimium creditis unicuique, Auct. ad : eorum animi molles et aetate fluxi dolis haud difficulter capiebantur,: Hecabe, Non oblita animorum, annorum oblita suorum,: Nihil est tam angusti animi tamque parvi, quam amare divitias,: sordidus atque animi parvi,; : Drusus animi fluxioris erat,.—
In particular, some one specific emotion, inclination, or passion (honorable or base; in this signif., in the poets and prose writers, very freq. in the plur.). —
Courage, spirit: ibi nostris animus additus est,; cf. ; : deficiens animo maesto cum corde jacebat,: virtute atque animo resistere,: fac animo magno fortique sis,fin.: Cassio animus accessit, et Parthis timor injectus est,: nostris animus augetur,: mihi in dies magis animus accenditur,; ; ; : Nunc demum redit animus,: bellica Pallas adest, Datque animos,: pares annis animisque,: cecidere illis animique manusque, (cf.: tela viris animusque cadunt,) et saep.—Hence, bono animo esse or uti, to be of good courage, : Am. Bono animo es. So. Scin quam bono animo sim? : In re malā animo si bono utare, adjuvat,: bono animo fac sis,: quin tu animo bono es,: quare bono animo es,; so ; ; so also, satis animi,sufficient courage,.—Also for hope: magnus mihi animus est, hodiernum diem initium libertatis fore,.—Trop., of the violent, stormy motion of the winds of Æolus: Aeolus mollitque animos et temperat iras,.—Of a top: dant animos plagae,give it new force, quicker motion,.— Of spirit in discourse: in Asinio Pollione et consilii et animi satis,. —
Haughtiness, arrogance, pride: quae civitas est in Asiā, quae unius tribuni militum animos ac spiritus capere possit? can bear the arrogance and pride, etc., : jam insolentiam norātis hominis: norātis animos ejus ac spiritus tribunicios,; so ; (cf.: quia paululum vobis accessit pecuniae, Sublati animi sunt,).—
Violent passion, vehemence, wrath: animum vincere, iracundiam cohibere, etc.,: animum rege, qui nisi paret Imperat,: qui dominatur animo suo,.—So often in plur.; cf οἱ θυμοί: ego meos animos violentos meamque iram ex pectore jam promam, : vince animos iramque tuam,; ; : Parce tuis animis, vita, nocere tibi,: Sic longius aevum Destruit ingentes animos,: coëunt sine more, sine arte, Tantum animis irāque,—
Moderation, patience, calmness, contentedness, in the phrase aequus animus, an even mind: si est animus aequos tibi,; ; ; and often in the abl., aequo animo, with even mind, patiently, etc.: aequo animo ferre,; ; ; ; : aequo animo esse,; ib. Judith, 7, 23: Aequo animo est? of merry heart (Gr. εὐθυμεῖ), : animis aequis remittere,: aequiore animo successorem opperiri,: haud aequioribus animis audire,: sapientissimus quisque aequissimo animo moritur; stultissimus iniquissimo. ; so ; ; : iniquo animo, Rib.; ; .—
Agreeable feeling, pleasure, delight: cubat amans animo obsequens,: indulgent animis, et nulla quid utile cura est,; so, esp. freq.: animi causā (in Plaut. once animi gratiā), for the sake of amusement, diversion (cf.: haec (animalia) alunt animi voluptatisque causā,): Post animi causā mihi navem faciam,; so ; : liberare fidicinam animi gratiā,: qui illud animi causā fecerit, hunc praedae causā quid facturum putabis?: habet animi causā rus amoenum et suburbanum, Matth.; cf. § 134, and Madv. ad ; : Romanos in illis munitionibus animine causā cotidie exerceri putatis?; Plin. praef. 17 Sill.—
Disposition toward any one: hoc animo in nos esse debebis, ut etc.,: meus animus erit in te semper, quem tu esse vis,fin.: qui, quo animo inter nos simus, ignorant,; so ; 5, 2: In quo in primis quo quisque animo, studio, benevolentiā fecerit, ponderandum est,: quod (Allobroges) nondum bono animo in populum Romanum viderentur,to be well disposed,—In the pregn. signif. of kind, friendly feeling, affection, kindness, liberality: animum fidemque praetorianorum erga se expertus est,: Nec non aurumque animusque Latino est,.—Hence, meton., of a person who is loved, my heart, my soul: salve, anime mi,: da, meus ocellus, mea rosa, mi anime, da, mea voluptas,; so ; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep. —
The power of willing, the will, inclination, desire, purpose, design, intention (syn.: voluntas, arbitrium, mens, consilium, propositum), ἡ βούλησις: qui rem publicam animo certo adjuverit, Rib.: pro inperio tuo meum animum tibi servitutem servire aequom censui,: Ex animique voluntate id procedere primum,goes forth at first from the inclination of the soul,; so, pro animi mei voluntate, (v. Manut. ad h.l.): teneo, quid animi vostri super hac re siet,; : Nam si semel tuom animum ille intellexerit, Prius proditurum te etc.,: Prius quam tuom ut sese habeat animum ad nuptias perspexerit,: Sin aliter animus voster est, ego etc.,: Quid mi istaec narras? an quia non audisti, de hac re animus meus ut sit?: qui ab auro gazāque regiā manus, oculos, animum cohibere possit,: istum exheredare in animo habebat,: nobis crat in animo Ciceronem ad Caesarem mittere, we had it in mind to send, etc., ; Serv. ad : hostes in foro constiterunt, hoc animo, ut, etc.,: insurrexerunt uno animo in Paulum,with one mind,; : persequi Jugurtham animus ardebat, Gerlach (others, animo, as Dietsch); so : in nova fert animus mutatas dicere formas, my mind inclines to tell of, etc., .—Hence, est animus alicui, with inf., to have a mind for something, to aim at, etc.: omnibus unum Opprimere est animus,: Sacra Jovi Stygio perficere est animus,: Fuerat animus conjuratis corpus occisi in Tiberim trahere,; ; cf. .—So, aliquid alicui in animo est, with inf., .—So, inducere in animum or animum, to resolve upon doing something; v. induco.—
Trop., of the principle of life and activity in irrational objects, as in Engl. the word mind is used.
Of brutes: in bestiis, quarum animi sunt rationis expertes,whose minds,: Sunt bestiae, in quibus etiam animorum aliquā ex parte motus quosdam videmus,: ut non inscite illud dictum videatur in sue, animum illi pecudi datum pro sale, ne putisceret,, ubi v. Madv.: (apes Ingentes animos angusto in pectore versant,: Illiusque animos, qui multos perdidit unus, Sumite serpentis,: cum pecudes pro regionis caelique statu et habitum corporis et ingenium animi et pili colorem gerant,: Umbria (boves progenerat) vastos nec minus probabiles animis quam corporibus, si equum ipsum nudum et solum corpus ejus et animum contemplamur, (so sometimes mens: iniquae mentis asellus,).—
Of plants: haec quoque Exuerint silvestrem animum, i. e. naturam, ingenium,their wild nature,.—
Transf. Of God or the gods, as we say, the Divine Mind, the Mind of God: certe et deum ipsum et divinum animum corpore liberatum cogitatione complecti possumus, (so mens, of God, ; ): Tantaene animis caelestibus irae?.

la:verb:animo.gloss: to fill with breath or air
senses: to fill with breath or air
to transform into a living being; to inspire
to give or bring life to; to make alive, to make or cause to live
to give spirit or vigor to
to give courage to; to encourage
to endow with spirit or courage
to endow with a particular disposition of mind; to rouse, incite
to give a particular disposition of mind to
la:verb:animo.html:
ănĭmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n.
anima and animus
.
Act.
To fill with breath or air (cf. anima, I. and II.): duas tibias uno spiritu,to blow upon,: bucinas,.—More freq.,
To quicken, animate (cf. anima, II. C.): quicquid est hoc, omnia animat, format, alit, auget, creat, Pac. ap. ; : vitaliter esse animata,: formare, figurare, colorare, animare,. stellae divinis animatae mentibus, ; . —
To endow with, to give, a particular temperament or disposition of mind (cf. animus, II. B. 1. b.): utcumque temperatus sit aër, ita pueros orientes animari atque formari, ex eoque ingenia, mores, animum fingi,: Mattiaci ipso terrae suae solo ac caelo acrius animantur, i. e. ferociores redduntur, are rendered more spirited, * .—
In Ovid in a pregnant signif.: aliquid in aliquid animare, to transform a lifeless object to a living being, to change into by giving life (cf. anima, II. C. 3.): guttas animavit in angues,: in Nymphas animatā classe marinas,.—
Trop., of colors, to enliven: si quid Apellei gaudent animāsse colores,.—Of torches, to light or kindle: animare ad crimina taxos,.—Sometimes = recreare, to refresh, revive: cibo potuque animavit,: florem,; so ; or in gen., to encourage, help: ope animari, Cod. Th. 6, 4, 21, § 3: copiis,.—And with inf. = incitare, to move, incite to: Ut hortatu vestro Eustathius, quae de scommate paulo ante dixerit, animetur aperire,.—Hence, ănĭmātus, a, um, P. a.
Animated (cf. anima, II. C.): virum virtute verā vivere animatum addecet, Enn. ap. .—
(Acc. to C.) Brought or put into a particular frame of mind, disposed, inclined, minded, in some way (freq. and class.): hoc animo decet animatos esse amatores probos,: avi et atavi nostri, quom allium ac caepe eorum verba olerent, tamen optime animati erant, Varr. ap. (where the play upon olere and animati is to be noticed): animatus melius quam paratus,better disposed than prepared,: socii infirme animati,: sic animati esse debetis, ut si ille adesset,: ut quem ad modum in se quisque, sic in amicum sit animatus,: insulas non nullas bene animatas confirmavit,well affected,; : male animatus erga principem exercitus,: circa aliquem,: hostili animo adversus rem publicam animatus,: animatus in necem alicujus, Macr S. 1, 11.—In Plaut. with inf.: si quid animatus es facere, Truc. 5, 74.—
Endowed with courage, courageous, stouthearted (cf. animus, II. 2. a. and animosus; only in ante-class. poetry): milites armati atque animati probe,: cum animatus iero, satis armatus sum, Att. ap. : hostis animatus, p. 233, 18.—* Sup. Auct. Itin. Alex. 13.— Adv. not used.—
Neutr., to be animate, living (cf. anima, II. C.); so only ănĭ-mans, antis (abl. com. animante, but animanti in ; gen. plur. animantium in Cic., animantum in Lucr., , and ),
P. a., animate, living: quos (deos) Vitellius ne animantes quidem esse concedat,: mundum ipsum animantem sapientemque esse,: animans composque rationis mundus est,. —Hence,
Subst., any living, animate being; an animal (orig. in a wider sense than animal, since it included men, animals, and plants; but usu., like that word, for animals in opp. to men. The gender varies in the best class. writers between masc., fem., and neutr. When it designates man, it is masc.; brutes, com. fem.; in its widest sense, it is neutr.): sunt quaedam, quae animam habent, nec sunt animalia, etc.,; ; : genus omne animantum,; so ; ; ; 1, 1038; 2, 78; 2, 880; 2, 921; 2, 943; 2, 1063; 2, 1071; 3, 266; 3, 417; 3, 720; 5, 431; 5, 855; 5, 917: animantium genera quattuor,; fin.: animantium aliae coriis tectae sunt, aliae villis vestitae, etc.,: cum ceteras animantes abjecisset ad pastum, solum hominem erexit,: animantia, quae sunt nobis nota,.—Of animals, living beings, as opp. to plants: Jam vero vites sic claviculis adminicula tamquam manibus adprehendunt atque ita se erigunt, ut animantes,.— Of man: hic stilus haud petet ultro Quemquam animantem, * .—Comp., sup., and adv. not used.
la:verb:animo.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n.

la:noun:anima.html:
ănĭma, ae, f. (
gen. animāï, ; et saep.; cf. Neue, Formenl. I. p. 12; Lachm. ad ; dat. and abl. plur. regul. animis, ; ; ; ; ; ; , 13, 18; 13, 19; : animabus, only in eccl. and later Lat.,; ; ; et saep.; ; ; , 19, 23; Prud. c. ; ; ; Neue, Formenl. I. p. 29) [v. animus], pr. that which blows or breathes; hence,
Lit., air, a current of air, a breeze, wind (mostly poet.): ne quid animae forte amittat dormiens,: vela ventorum animae immittere, Att. ap. (Trag. Rel. p. 137 Rib.): aurarum leves animae,: prece quaesit Ventorum pavidus paces animasque secundas,he anxiously implores a lull in the winds and a favoring breeze,: impellunt animae lintea,: Ne dubites quin haec animaï turbida sit vis,: Quantum ignes animaeque

valent (of the wind in the workshop of Vulcan), .—Also of a flame of fire (blowing like the air): noctilucam tollo, ad focum fero, inflo; anima reviviscit, Varr. ap. .—

Transf.
In gen., the air, as an element, like fire, water, and earth (mostly poet.): aqua, terra, anima et sol, Enn. ap. : qui quattuor ex rebus posse omnia rentur, Ex igni, terrā atque animā, procrescere et imbri,: ut, quem ad modum ignis animae, sic anima aquae, quodque anima aquae, id aqua terrae proportione redderet. Earum quattuor rerum etc.,: utrum (animus) sit ignis, an anima, an sanguis,: si anima est (animus), fortasse dissipabitur,; : si deus aut anima aut ignis est, idem est animus hominis,: animus ex inflammatā animā constat, ut potissimum videri video Panaetio,: Semina terrarumque animaeque,.—
The air inhaled and exhaled, breath (concr.); while spiritus denotes orig. breathing (abstr.; very freq. in prose and poetry); cf. : excipiat animam eam, quae ducta sit spiritu,: animam compressi, aurem admovi, Ruhnk.: animam recipe,take breath,: cum spiritus ejus (sc. Demosthenis) esset angustior, tantum continendā animā in dicendo est assecutus, ut, etc.,: ne circuitus ipse verborum sit longior quam vires atque anima patiatur,; 3, 46, 181; : fetida anima nasum oppugnat, Titin. ap. (Com. Rel. p. 136 Rib.); : qui non modo animum integrum, sed ne animam quidem puram conservare potuisset,: animas et olentia Medi Ora fovent illo, with this the Medes correct their breath, etc., : respiramen iterque Eripiunt animae,; cf. : animae gravitas,bad smell of the breath,; cf. ; : artavit clusitque animam,; so : spes illorum abominatio animae,.—Of breath exhaled: inspirant graves animas,.— Of the air breathed into a musical instrument, a breath of air, Varr. ap. . 13.—Since air is a necessary condition of life,
The vital principle, the breath of life: animus est, quo sapimus, anima, quā vivimus, (hence anima denotes the animal principle of life, in distinction from animus, the spiritual, reasoning, willing principle; very freq. in Lucr. and class.): Mater est terra, ea parit corpus, animam aether adjugat, Pac. ap. (Trag. Rel. p. 88 Rib.): tunc cum primis ratione sagaci, Unde anima atque animi constet natura, videndum,whence spring life and the nature of the mind,; sq.; so ; ; ; 2, 950; 4, 922; 4, 944; 4, 959; 6, 798; 6, 1223; 6, 1233 et saep.: deus totus est sensuus, totus visuus, totus audituus, totus animae, totus animi, totus sui, Jan: quaedam (animantia) animum habent, quaedam tantum animam,: anima omnis carnis in sanguine est,—Hence,
In gen., life: cum anima corpus liquerit, Rib.: Animae pauxillulum in me habet, Rib.: Date ferrum, quī me animā privem, Enn. ap. (Trag. Rel. p. 37 Rib.): me dicabo atque animam devōvo (i. e. devovero) hostibus, Att. ap. (Trag. Rel. p. 283 Rib.): conficit animam vis volneris, Rib.: adimere animam,; so : exstinguere,: relinquere,: edere,: de vestrā vitā, de conjugum vestrarum ac liberorum animā judicandum est,: si tibi omnia sua praeter animam tradidit,: libertas et anima nostra in dubio est,: pauci, quibus relicta est anima, clausi in tenebris, etc.,; cf. retinere,: de manu viri et fratris ejus requiram animam hominis,; ; : animam agere,to give up the ghost, to die,; so also efflare,to expire,; ; ; so, exhalare,; and, exspirare, (cf. in Gr. θυμὸν ἀποπνέειν, ψυχὴν ἐκπνέειν, βίον ἀποψύχειν, etc.): deponere,: ponere,; : amittere,: emittere, Br. (so in Gr. ἀφιέναι τὴν ψυχήν): proicere,: purpuream vomit ille animam, said of a wounded man,.—In and 26, anima in v. 25 seems to pass to the higher meaning, soul, (cf. infra, II. D.) in v. 26, as ἡ ψυχή in the original also can do.—Poet.: anima amphorae,the fumes of wine,: Ni ego illi puteo, si occepso, animam omnem intertraxero, draw up all the life of that well, i. e. draw it dry, .—Trop.: corpus imperii unius praesidis nutu, quasi animā et mente, regeretur,: accentus quasi anima vocis est, Lind.—Prov.: animam debere, to owe life itself, of one deeply in debt: quid si animam debet? (Graecum proverbium: καὶ αὐτὴν τὴν ψυχὴν ὀφείλει, Don.).—Metaph., applied to plants and other things possessing organic life, ; so ; ; —
Meton., a creature endowed with anima, a living being: ova parere solet genu' pennis condecoratum, non animam, Enn. ap. : hi (deos) fibris animāque litant,; ; ; ; et saep.: animae rationis expertes,.—So esp. of men (as we also say souls for persons;poet. or in post-Aug. prose): egregias animas, quae sanguine nobis Hanc patriam peperere suo, etc.,: animae quales nec candidiores, etc.,; : vos Treveri et ceterae servientium animae,ministering spirits,.—So in enumerations in eccl. Lat.: hos genuit Jacob sedecim animas,; ; ; .—Of slaves (eccl. Lat.): merces animarum hominum, (after the use of ἡ ψυχή and ). —Hence, also, souls separated from the body, the shades of the Lower World, manes: Unde (ex Averno) animae excitantur, Enn. ap. : tu pias laetis animas reponis Sedibus,; cf. : animamque sepulcro Condimus,; ; so ; 10, 41; 14, 411; 15, 158; ; so, vita: tenuīs sine corpore vitas volitare,.—So in eccl. Lat. of departed spirits: timete eum, qui potest animam et corpus perdere in Gehennam, bis: non derelinques animam meam in Inferno,; ; .—
As expressive of love: vos, meae carissimae animae,my dearest souls,; : Pro quā non metuam mori, Si parcent animae fata superstiti,the dear surviving life,; cf.: animae dimidium meae,: meae pars animae,.—
Sometimes for animus, as the rational soul of man.
The mind as the seat of thought (cf. animus, II. A.): anima rationis consiliique particeps,: causa in animā sensuque meo penitus affixa atque insita,: ingenii facinora, sicut anima, immortalia sunt,.—So often in eccl. Lat.: ad te Domine, levavi animam meam,; ; : magnificat anima mea Dominum,; —
As the seat of feeling (cf. animus, II. B.): sapimus animo, fruimur animā: sine animo anima est debilis, Att. ap. (Trag. Rel. p. 175 Rib.): desiderat anima mea ad te, Deus,: tristis est anima mea,; et saep.—
For consciousness (cf. animus, II. A. 3. and conscientia, II. A.): cum perhibetur animam liquisse,; in this phrase animus is more common.

la:noun:animadversio.html:
ănĭmadversĭo, ōnis, f.
animadverto
,
the perception or observation of an object; consideration, attention (in good prose, most freq. in Cic.).
In gen.: notatio naturae et animadversio peperit artem,: hoc totum est sive artis sive animadversionis sive consuetudinis,; so —Hence, in reference to one's self, self-inspection, watchfulness: excitanda animadversio et diligentia, ut ne quid temere agamus,; and in gen. inquiry: quaestio atque animadversio in aliquem,. —
Esp.
Reproach, censure: nec effugere possemus animadversionem, si, etc.,.—
Chastisement, punishment: animadversio Dollabellae in audaces servos,: paterna,: omnis autem animadversio et castigatio contumeliā vacare debet,; so ; : in proelium exarsere, ni valens animadversione paucorum oblitos jam Batavos imperii admonuisset, * ; ; —So of the punishment decreed by the censors for crime committed (usu. called nota censoria): notiones animadversionesque censorum, B. and K.: censoriae,; cf. .—And by the dictator: dictatoria,; cf. Bremi.

la:verb:animadverto.gloss: to pay attention, attend, focus, concentrate, give heed to, consider, regard, observe
senses: to pay attention, attend, focus, concentrate, give heed to, consider, regard, observe
la:verb:animadverto.html:
ănĭmadverto (archaic -vorto), ti, sum, 3, v. a.
contr. from animum adverto, which orthography is very freq. in the anteclass. period; cf. adverto, II. B.
(scarcely found in any poet beside Ter. and Verg.),
to direct the mind or attention to a thing, to attend to, give heed to, to take heed, consider, regard, observe.
Lit.
In gen.: alios tuam rem credidisti magis quam tete animum advorsuros,: atque haec in bello plura et majora videntur timentibus, eadem non tam animadvertuntur in pace,: sed animadvertendum est diligenter, quae natura rerum sit,: dignitas tua facit, ut animadvertatur quicquid facias,; .—With ut, to think of: illud me non animadvertisse moleste ferrem, ut ascriberem, etc., (cf.: animos advertere, ne,).—
Esp., as t. t.
Of the lictor, whose duty it was to give attention, to see, that the consul, when he appeared, should receive due homage (cf. ; Schwarz ad , and Smith, Dict. Antiq., s. v. lictor): consul animadvertere proximum lictorem jussit,—
Of the people, to whom the lictor gave orders to pay attention, to pay regard to: consule theatrum introeunte, cum lictor animadverti ex more jussisset, Ruhnk.—
Transf., as a consequence of attention.
To remark, notice, observe, perceive, see (in a more general sense than above; the most usu. signif. of this word).
With acc.: Ecquid attendis? ecquid animadvertis horum silentium?: utcumque animadversa aut existimata erunt, Liv. praef. med.: his animadversis,; et saep.: Equidem etiam illud animadverto, etc., Beier.: nutrix animadvertit puerum dormientem circumplicatum serpentis amplexu,.—
With acc. and inf.: postquam id vos velle animum advorteram,: qui non animadverterit innocentes illos natos, etc.,: turrim conlucere animadvertit,.—
With ind. quest.: quod quale sit, etiam in bestiis quibusdam animadverti potest, Cic.Am. 8, 27.—
In a pregn. sense, to discern something, or, in gen., to apprehend, understand, comprehend, know (less freq. than the synn. cognoscere, intellegere, etc.): boni seminis sues animadvertuntur a facie et progenie,: nonne animadvertis, quam multi effugerint?: ut adsint, cognoscant, animadvertant, quid de religione ... existimandum sit,: animadverti enim et didici ex tuis litteris te, etc.,.—
To notice a wrong, to censure, blame, chastise, punish (cf. the Engl. phrase to attend to one, for to punish): Ea primum ab illo animadvortenda injuriast,deserves to be punished, (animadvortenda = castiganda, vindicanda, Don.): O facinus animadvortendum,O crime worthy of punishment,: animadvertenda peccata,: res a magistratibus animadvertenda,: neque animadvertere neque vincire nisi sacerdotibus permissum = morte multare,to punish with death,.—Esp. freq. in judicial proceedings as t. t., constr. with in aliquem: qui institueras

animadvertere in eos, : imperiti, si in hunc animadvertissem, crudeliter et regie factum esse dicerent,: qui in alios animadvertisset indictā causā,; so ; : in Marcianum Icelum, ut in libertum, palam animadversum,; ; ; 4, 49; ; ; ; ; ; hence, effect for cause, animadverti,to offend, be censurable,.

la:noun:animula.html:
ănĭmŭla, ae, f.dim.
anima
,
a little soul, life: aegra et saucia, Auct. ap. (Hertz, anima): mulierculae, Sulp. ap. : vagula, blandula, etc., Hadr. Imp. ap. ; so and 4761; .

la:noun:animal.html:
ănĭmăl, ālis (abl. animali; but Rhem. Palaem. p. 1372 P. gives animale), n.
as if for animale, which is found in MS.; ; cf. animalis
,
a living being, an animal.
In the widest sense, ζῶον (cf. ζωός = living): inanimum est omne, quod pulsu agitatur externo, quod autem est animal, id motu cietur interiore et suo,, where it is opp. to the adj. inanimum, and therefore is equivalent to animale; cf. : uti possint sentire animalia quaeque,: cum omne animal patibilem naturam habeat, etc.,; : formicae, animal minumum,; et saep.—Of men: animal providum et sagax homo,; so : sanctius his animal,: bicipites hominum aliorumve animalium,: (Vitellius) umbraculis hortorum abditus, ut ignava animalia, quibus cibum suggeras, jacent torpentque,; : etiam fera animalia, si clausa teneas, virtutis obliviscuntur,; : animalia maris,; .—Also of the universe, considered as an animated existence: hunc mundum animal esse, idque intellegens et divinā providentiā constitutum,; .—
Sometimes in a more restricted sense, as antith. to man, a beast (as in Heb. , animal, from , to live): multa ab animalium vocibus tralata in homines,: alia animalia gradiendo, alia serpendo, etc.,: animalia inusitata ceteris gentibus, nisi invecta,; : si quod animal in mustum inciderit,: si quod animal aurem intraverit,: similitudo non ab hominibus modo petitur, verum etiam ab animalibus,.—Hence, with contempt, of a man: funestum illud animal, ex nefariis stupris concretum,that pernicious brute,.

la:adj:animalis.html:
ănĭmālis, e, adj.
anima
.
Consisting of air, aërial (cf. anima, I. and II. A.): simplex est natura animantis, ut vel terrena vel ignea vel animalis vel umida,: naturam esse quattuor omnia gignentium corporum ... terrena et humida ... reliquae duae partes, una ignea, altera animalis,: animalis spirabilisque natura, cui nomen est aër (B. and K.; others read animabilis),: spirabilis, id est animalis,.—
Animate, living (cf. anima, II. C.).
In gen.: corpora,: pulli,: colligata corpora vinculis animalibus,: intellegentia,: ut mutum in simulacrum ex animali exemplo veritas transferatur,from the living original,.—
In the lang. of sacrifice: hostia animalis,an offering of which only the life is consecrated to the gods, but the flesh is destined for the priests and others,; ; .—Dii animales, gods who were formerly men, .—* Adv.ănĭmālĭter, like an animal (opp. spiritualiter): animaliter vivere,.

la:adj:anilis.gloss: of or pertaining to an old woman
senses: of or pertaining to an old woman
la:adj:anilis.html:
ănīlis, e, adj.
anus
,
of or pertaining to an old woman.
Lit.: voltus,: passus,: aetas,.—
Often in a contemptuous sense, like an old woman, old womanish, anile: ineptiae paene aniles,: superstitio imbecilli animi atque anilis,; so ; ; * ; .—Comp. and sup. not used.—* Adv.: ănīlĭter, like an old woman: dicere aliquid,.

la:adj:animaequus.html:
ănĭm-aequus, a, um, adj.
animus
,
not easily moved; also of good courage (eccl. Lat.): animaequior esto,; : animaequiores estote filii,; ; .

senses: courageous/full of courage, brave, bold, undaunted
la:adj:animosus.html:
ănĭmōsus, a, um, adj.
anima
.
Full of air, airy (cf. anima, I. and II. A.): guttura,through which the breath passes,.—Of the wind. blowing violently: Eurus,: ventus,.—
Full of life, living, animate, of pictures, etc. (cf. anima, II. C.): Gloria Lysippost animosa effingere signa,.—Comp., sup., and adv. of 1. animosus not used.

senses: full of life, alive, living, animated

senses: The act of animating or giving life to, animation.

la:noun:animatio.html:
ănĭmātĭo, ōnis, f.
animo
,

Lit.: arboris,.—
Meton., concr., a living being: divinae animationis species, * .

senses: A living thing or creature, an animal (as opposed to plants; as opposed to a man)

senses: Derived from animus: courageousness/courage, bravery, boldness, undauntedness
Derived from animus: arrogance, haughtiness, pridefulness
Derived from animus: aggressiveness, ardor, fervor, passion, vehemence
Derived from animus: enmity, fury/furiosity/furiousness, wrath/wrathfulness
Derived from animus: adamancy, headstrongness, wilfulness
Certain particular strong emotions: animosity, enmity, hostility, opposition
la:noun:animositas.html:
ănĭmōsĭtas, ātis, f.
animosus
(only post-class.).
Boldness, courage, spirit: resistendi,: equi,. —
Vehemence, impetuosity, ardor, ; in plur., * ; , and Civ. Dei, 14, 2 al.—
Wrath, enmity (eccl. Lat.): iracundia animositatis illius (Dei) subversio illius est,; ; .
